insp1-the-plague-in-the-walls.reason: Opens by promising a seven-step inspection; who looks first (owner reports a suspicion, the priest looks) and why the house is emptied only come out step by step; ends on the walk-away exercise, not the answer.
insp1-the-plague-in-the-walls.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Before you sign, who looks first? In Leviticus 14 the owner speaks first, but only as a suspicion, "It seemeth to me", and someone appointed to look comes to see before anything is settled. And before he walks in, the house is emptied, so the inspection itself harms nothing in it. Then come five more steps: clear signs, a wait and a second look, a targeted repair, a re-check, and a walk-away point decided in advance. Here is how the Word lays them out.
insp1-the-plague-in-the-walls.example: ONE DAMP BASEMENT, SEVEN STEPS. Say a family is weighing a house and notices a musty smell downstairs. They report it as a suspicion, not a verdict: something may be wet. They have the stored boxes moved off the wall before anyone looks, so the report is about the wall and not the boxes. They write down what they are looking for as signs they can point to: a stain line, a soft spot. They arrange a second look after the next week of rain. And before they fall in love with the kitchen, they write down the finding that would make them walk away.
insp1-the-plague-in-the-walls.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Before you sign, who looks first? Someone appointed to look, after the owner has honestly named a suspicion and after the house has been cleared so the looking does no harm. Then the looking follows Yahweh's order: visible signs written down, time and a second look, the affected stones and no more, a re-check of the repair, and a stopping point named before anyone is attached. The procedure is His, and it carries no verdict on the family whose walls are damp. Run those seven steps before you sign, and you will be ahead of most buyers alive.

teen.open: Before you sign for a house, who should look first? In Leviticus 14 someone looks carefully before anything is decided, and the house is emptied first so the inspection hurts nothing.
teen.close: So who looks first? A careful looker, after an honest report, in a cleared house. Then look again, fix only what is bad, check the fix, and know when you would walk away.

senior.open: The title asks who should look before a purchase is signed. Leviticus 14 answers with an order: the owner raises a suspicion honestly, the house is emptied so nothing is harmed, and an appointed person looks against signs that can be pointed to.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. Before you sign, someone appointed to look goes in after an honest report and a cleared house, looks twice, repairs in proportion, checks the repair, and knows beforehand the point at which the answer is to walk away.

insp2-i-viewed-the-walls.reason: Opens with the plain answer (LOOK, then SPEAK) and the closing paragraph lands it: before you say anything, go look yourself, go where the easy route will not, and write down only what you saw.

insp3-see-the-land-what-it-is.reason: Opens on the design of the Numbers 13 brief; why a sharp brief matters (answerable, comparable pairs) and why a sample matters (it ends the argument about facts) arrive mid-lesson; the end lands only the sample half.
insp3-see-the-land-what-it-is.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does an inspection need a sharp brief and something to bring back? Because a vague instruction brings home opinions that cannot be compared, while short paired questions, like strong or weak and fat or lean, bring home answers anyone can check. And a sample carried home in the hand ends the argument about the facts, so the argument moves to the decision, where it belongs. Numbers 13 shows both in one brief.
insp3-see-the-land-what-it-is.example: TWO WAYS TO SEND A FRIEND. Say you ask a friend to look at a house for you. Sent with go and tell me what you think, he comes back with a feeling: it seemed fine, a bit tired. Sent with six pairs written down, dry or damp, level or moving, one roof layer or three, original panel or replaced, serviced or not, sound or failing, he comes back with six answers you can lay beside the next house. And if he also brings the photo of the furnace plate with the year on it, nobody argues about the furnace. You argue only about what to do.
insp3-see-the-land-what-it-is.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why a sharp brief and something to bring back? Because the quality of a report is set before the inspector leaves. Moses sent twelve men with six answerable pairs, few enough to carry, and told them to bring of the fruit. They came home showing the fruit, and nobody ever disputed the grapes; what went wrong was the decision. Write your six pairs before the visit, ask for something carried home, and what you get back is a report, not a story.

teen.open: Why does a home inspection need clear questions and proof? Clear questions get answers you can check, and proof like a photo stops the arguing about what is true.
teen.close: So the answer is simple. Ask a few sharp questions that cannot be shrugged at, and bring something back. Then you can argue about what to do, not about what is there.

senior.open: The title asks why an inspection needs a sharp brief and a sample. Numbers 13 shows that paired, answerable questions produce findings that can be compared, and that evidence carried home settles the facts.
senior.close: So the answer stands plainly. Write a short brief of answerable pairs before anyone goes, and require something brought back. Then the facts are settled by the evidence, and the discussion that remains is the decision itself.

insp4-two-reports-one-land.reason: The answer (keep observation whole, label conclusions as conclusions, keep feeling out of the findings) only arrives near the end after a long walk through Numbers 13-14; opening frames the distinction without stating it.
insp4-two-reports-one-land.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How do you keep a report honest when fear starts writing the conclusions? Keep three things apart. What you saw goes down whole, the hard parts included. What you concluded is written as a conclusion, clearly labelled. And what you felt stays out of the findings altogether. In Numbers 13 all twelve men saw the same true facts; ten let their dread pass as a finding, and the Word calls that an evil report.
insp4-two-reports-one-land.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How do you keep a report honest when fear starts writing the conclusions? Do what Joshua and Caleb did: keep every hard fact intact, add nothing that was not seen, and leave out nothing that was true, including that the LORD was with them. Draw the line down the page: what you observed on the left, what you concluded, feared or assumed on the right. Then hand in the left column and one clearly labelled recommendation. That line is the whole distance between a true report and an evil one.

teen.open: How do you keep a report honest when you are scared? Write what you actually saw, and keep your fear and guesses out of it.
teen.close: So here is the answer. Facts on one side, feelings and guesses on the other. Turn in the facts and one clearly marked suggestion. That keeps fear from writing your report.

senior.open: The title asks how a report stays honest when fear begins to shape its conclusions. Numbers 13 answers by separating what was observed from what was inferred and from what was felt.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. Keep the observation whole, label the conclusion as a conclusion, and keep the feeling out of the findings. That is what Caleb did, and it is the difference Scripture draws between a faithful report and an evil one.

insp6-man-looketh-on-the-outward-appeara.reason: The answer (appearance is real information but never sufficient; hold no conclusion with more confidence than its evidence earns) is spread through the middle; it ends on a homework list, not the answer.
insp6-man-looketh-on-the-outward-appeara.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Samuel's certain glance teach a home buyer? That what your eyes see is real information, and none of it is enough. Fresh paint is a true fact about the paint, not yet about the wall. Samuel, a prophet on a commission from Yahweh, was sure about Eliab on sight and was wrong. The answer is not to close your eyes but to judge righteous judgment (John 7:24): more evidence, not less.
insp6-man-looketh-on-the-outward-appeara.example: ONE PAINTED WALL. Say you walk into a house and the basement wall is freshly painted and spotless. Name the conclusion out loud: this basement is dry. Ask what it would take to actually know it: the seller's disclosure in writing, a moisture reading, a look after rain, a question to the neighbour. Then either get that, or write down plainly, I believe this basement is dry but I have not confirmed it. Either way you are no longer running on the paint.
insp6-man-looketh-on-the-outward-appeara.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Samuel's glance teach every home buyer? Your eyes are right about the paint and not yet about the wall. If a prophet could be certain and wrong, so can you, and the cure is not to stop looking but to look further. Name the conclusion you drew from appearance, ask what it would take to know it, and get that or write down that you have not. The failure is holding a conclusion with more confidence than its evidence earns. Close that gap where being wrong would cost the most.

teen.open: What does Samuel teach someone buying a house? What you see is real, but it is not the whole story. A nice paint job does not prove a good wall.
teen.close: So the answer is this. Trust your eyes for what they show, then check the rest. Do not be more sure than your proof lets you be.

senior.open: The title promises a lesson from Samuel for anyone buying a home. Samuel was certain on sight and mistaken, and the Lord's correction teaches that appearance is genuine information but never sufficient by itself.
senior.close: So the teaching comes to this. Treat what you see as a fact about the appearance, then seek the document, measurement or witness that tells you about the thing itself. Hold each conclusion only as firmly as its evidence allows.

insp8-prove-all-things.reason: Opens on 1 Thessalonians 5:21; the plain answer (no, the Bereans who checked Paul are called noble, and checking is how trust is earned) arrives in the second movement; ends on two exercises.
insp8-prove-all-things.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is checking everything really disloyal? No. The Bereans checked even the apostle Paul against the Scriptures every day, and the Word calls them more noble for it (Acts 17:11). Checking is not distrust; it is the road to trust that can bear weight. In 2 Kings 22:7 the workmen were no longer reckoned with because they dealt faithfully, a trust that rested on a record. Here is how the Word joins the two.
insp8-prove-all-things.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is checking everything really disloyal? The Word says the opposite. Prove all things and hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21); test against the Word, not your own feeling; and let a faithful record earn the trust that retires the reckoning, as it did for Josiah's workmen, and only where it has truly been earned. Checking is how trust stops resting on a feeling and starts resting on something. That is loyalty with its eyes open, and it honors the people who prove faithful.

teen.open: Is it disloyal to check what people tell you? No. The Bible calls the people who checked Paul's teaching noble.
teen.close: So checking is not disloyal. It is how real trust gets built. When someone proves faithful over time, you can trust them, and you know why.

senior.open: The title asks whether checking everything is a form of disloyalty. Acts 17:11 answers no: those who searched the Scriptures daily to test Paul's teaching are called more noble.
senior.close: So the question is answered. Checking is the path to trust, not its enemy. A faithful record, observed over time, is what allows trust to rest on something solid, and that kind of trust is worth telling the faithful person about.

insp5-they-came-to-search-it-out.reason: Opens on scoping a survey down; why the decisive thing about a property often cannot be measured (the spies' finding was about the people, learned by lodging and listening) arrives only near the end.
insp5-they-came-to-search-it-out.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why can the most important thing about a home often not be measured? Because it lives in what people who have been there already know. The two spies sent to Jericho came back with four lines, and they said nothing about the famous walls. Their finding was about the people, who were fainting with fear, and they learned it by lodging in a house and listening. No tape measure or photograph could have reached it.
insp5-they-came-to-search-it-out.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why is the most important thing about a home often not a measurement? Because, like the spies' report from Jericho, the decisive finding is often what a person who has lived there for years already knows: about the water, the road, the survey stake, what the basement does in March. It costs twenty minutes at a fence and a willingness to ask. So scope your look to the one question that would change your decision, answer it properly, and report all things that befell you, including the parts you could not reach.

teen.open: Why can the most important thing about a house be impossible to measure? Because often it is something the neighbours know, not something a tape measure finds.
teen.close: So the answer is to ask people. The spies learned the key fact by listening, not by measuring walls. Ask the neighbour, and be honest about what you could not check.

senior.open: The title asks why the most decisive thing about a home is often beyond measurement. The spies at Jericho show it: their finding concerned the people, and it came from lodging in a house and listening.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. The deciding fact is frequently held by those who have lived nearby for years, and it is found by asking patiently. Narrow your look to the one question that matters, and report fully, including what you could not see.

insp7-he-digged-deep.reason: Why inspect the foundation first (invisible on a clear day, fails all at once) and why haste is a warning (Isaiah 28:16) are built up across the lesson; it ends on the one-specialist exercise rather than the answer.
insp7-he-digged-deep.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why inspect the foundation first, and why is rushing a warning sign? Because a house without a foundation looks exactly like a house with one on a clear day; the difference shows only under load, and then it fell immediately (Luke 6:49). Yahweh's own cornerstone was a tried stone, tested before it was laid, and the same verse says he that believeth shall not make haste (Isaiah 28:16). When you are being hurried past the hidden part, that is data.
insp7-he-digged-deep.example: ONE SPECIALIST, TWO CHOICES. Say a household can afford exactly one specialist, and the seller's agent says another offer is coming tomorrow. The tired kitchen is what everyone keeps talking about, so spending the specialist there feels right. But the kitchen is already visible to your own eyes. The structure, the water and the electrical are not. Spend him under the house, and treat the deadline as one more reason to look, not one less.
insp7-he-digged-deep.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why inspect the foundation first, and why is rushing a warning? Because the part nobody photographs is the part that decides whether the house stands, and it gives no warning season before it fails. Yahweh tried His cornerstone before He laid it, and a man standing on something tried does not have to hurry. So spend your attention in the order of what decides, not what shows, and when you are pressed to skip the hidden part, slow down. And remember the greater foundation the parable is about: hearing His sayings and doing them.

teen.open: Why check a house's foundation before anything else? Because a bad foundation looks fine until a storm hits. And if someone rushes you, that is a warning.
teen.close: So the answer is to look under the house first and not let anyone hurry you past it. Jesus used this picture for something bigger too: hearing His words and doing them.

senior.open: The title asks why the foundation should be inspected first, and why haste should trouble us. Luke 6 shows a house that looked sound until the flood, and Isaiah 28 shows Yahweh testing His cornerstone before laying it.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Give your first attention and your one specialist to what decides whether the house stands, and treat pressure to hurry as information. The same parable reminds us the truest foundation is hearing the Lord and doing what He says.
